analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges from using federal student aid dollars for advertising, marketing, and recruiting.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 17, 2018, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never advanced before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop colleges — including for-profit schools — from spending revenue that comes from federal student aid, military and veterans' education benefits, and workforce grants on ads, marketing campaigns, and recruiting. That means no federal money for TV, radio, and internet advertising, no paying third parties to gather student contact information, and no paying recruiters to hunt for prospective students. Schools that get most of their money from federal education funds would have to report their marketing spending each year, with an independent auditor confirming compliance. The point is to keep federal aid dollars — which come from taxpayers and from students who have to repay loans — going to education rather than enrollment sales pitches.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and taxpayers benefit. Prospective students would see fewer aggressive sales pitches funded by their own federal aid dollars, and borrowers and taxpayers would not be underwriting college advertising budgets. Veterans and service members using education benefits would also be protected, since those funds are covered too.

how_it_helps.text: It bars colleges from using federal educational assistance funds — including Title IV student aid, military and veterans' education benefits, and workforce grants — for advertising, marketing, or recruiting activities [S2, S3].
Covered activities include paid ads on TV, radio, billboards, and online, buying leads from third parties, and paying staff or contractors to identify and attract prospective students [S3].

Schools that get 65% or more of their revenue from federal education funds would have to report their marketing and recruiting spending to the Education Department and Congress each year, verified by an independent auditor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges that rely heavily on federal education funds — especially for-profit institutions — would bear the cost, losing their ability to use taxpayer-backed dollars for advertising, lead purchasing, and recruiting staff, and taking on annual auditing and reporting requirements. Advertising and marketing firms that sell to colleges would also lose business.

drawbacks.text: The ban could reach ordinary admissions and advising work — paying staff who contact prospective students by phone or email is a covered activity [S3] — so legitimate schools would face compliance costs, and schools might simply shift marketing spending to non-federal revenue, which the bill expressly leaves untouched [S3].

Enforcement depends on a paper trail: only schools deriving 65% or more of revenue from federal aid must file annual reports with independent audit verification [S3], so the rule relies on self-certification rather than an active policing mechanism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it would stop schools that depend heavily on federal student aid from spending that money on ads and recruiting, which is where aggressive enrollment practices have historically drained student and taxpayer dollars. The main cost is a compliance burden — institutions would need auditors and annual certifications, and the rules could sweep in some routine admissions work (contacting applicants, advising) at legitimate schools, not just bad actors. The enforcement tool is blunt but the reporting requirement is a reasonable safeguard. Overall, the benefits to students and taxpayers outweigh the compliance costs, though the bill would have been stronger with clearer thresholds for which activities count.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate's education committee in December 2018, and with only weeks left in the session nothing happened — no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only actions were introduction and referral to the Senate HELP Committee on December 17, 2018 [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].
Because a bill must pass both chambers within the same two-year Congress, the measure died at the end of the session and would have to be reintroduced from scratch [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges — particularly for-profit schools — that draw heavily on federal student aid, military and veterans' education benefits, and workforce grants came out ahead, since they remain free to spend those dollars on advertising and recruiting. Students and taxpayers, whom the bill was meant to shield, are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges that rely on federal aid revenue

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 17, 2018 to bar colleges from using federal education aid revenue for recruiting and marketing [S1, S3].

for.name: Sens. Chris Murphy, Richard Blumenthal, Dick Durbin, and Tom Carper
for.role: U.S. Senators (CT, CT, IL, DE), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all four were Democrats, and no Republicans signed on [S4].

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 17, 2018 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S1, S5].

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the action history shows no committee activity after referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support — a sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans — and never advanced far enough for a vote that would show how the parties split [S4].

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and other schools heavily reliant on federal student aid
industries.note: These schools depend on Title IV aid, GI Bill benefits, and workforce grants for most of their revenue, and some have used large shares of it on advertising and lead-buying to enroll students. The bill would force them to fund recruiting from private revenue and report their marketing spending annually.
Colleges are big buyers of ads and third-party lead-generation services; a funding ban would shrink that business, though schools could still market using other revenue.

industries.industry: Private student loan and education services firms indirectly tied to enrollment growth
industries.note: Any slowdown in aggressive recruiting modestly reduces the enrollment pipelines these adjacent industries feed on; the bill does not directly regulate them.
